analysis.one_liner: Blocks new offshore oil and gas drilling along the Atlantic coast and off western Florida for ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had bipartisan support, never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the federal government from selling or preparing to sell any new offshore oil and gas leases through June 2029 in four Atlantic planning areas, the Straits of Florida, and the part of the eastern Gulf of Mexico within 125 miles of Florida's coast. Its aim was to shield coastal economies that depend on fishing, tourism, and clean beaches from the risk of drilling and spills. Existing leases were untouched. It was never taken up by the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities along the Atlantic seaboard and Florida's Gulf coast whose economies rest on tourism, commercial and recreational fishing, and clean beaches. Those industries are exposed to economic damage and lost property value when drilling activity or a spill comes to their waters. Homeowners and coastal businesses also benefit from reduced spill risk.

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management from offering any tract for oil and gas leasing or preleasing, or related activity, through June 30, 2029, in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas and the eastern Gulf of Mexico within 125 miles of Florida [S2][S3].
It does this by amending the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, writing the moratorium into law so it cannot be reversed by a future administration's leasing plan [S3].
It leaves existing leases alone, so it only blocks new drilling activity, not activity already under way [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that would have bid for new leases in the Atlantic and eastern Gulf planning areas bear the cost of foregone access. The federal government forgoes potential lease revenue, though leases could still be sold elsewhere in the Gulf of Mexico.

drawbacks.text: Blocking new leases forecloses domestic energy production and the federal royalties that leasing in those waters could have generated [S2].
The ten-year deadline of June 30, 2029 means the protection is temporary; Congress would have to act again to keep the waters off-limits [S2][S3].
Existing leases are expressly unaffected, so any drilling already authorized before enactment would continue [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded access to a small slice of potential new drilling areas for protection of large, established coastal economies — tourism, fishing, and waterfront property — that a spill or heavy industrial presence could damage permanently. The moratorium was time-limited and grandfathered existing leases, which moderates the cost to producers but also means the protection was not permanent. For the coastal states involved, the protection outweighed the foregone leasing revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Joe Cunningham introduced the bill on January 8, 2019, with Florida Republican Francis Rooney, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1][S3].
Nine members cosponsored it, a bipartisan group including two Republicans [S4].

On February 5, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress; the Natural Resources Committee never reported it, and the House never voted on it [S5].
The bill expired with the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests are better off because the bill died: the Atlantic and eastern Gulf planning areas it covered remained eligible for consideration in federal leasing plans, and no new legal barrier to drilling there was enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore drilling interests, not coastal economies

for.name: Rep. Joe Cunningham
for.role: Sponsor; Representative from South Carolina's 1st District, a coastal district
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a ten-year moratorium on new offshore drilling off the Atlantic coast and near Florida

for.name: Rep. Francis Rooney
for.role: Original cosponsor; Republican Representative from southwest Florida
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only original cosponsor at introduction

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on February 5, 2019 and never brought it to a markup or reported it to the House

against.name: Trump administration
against.what_they_did: In January 2019 proposed a five-year offshore leasing plan that would open Atlantic waters to drilling for the first time in decades, creating the backdrop for this bill

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but small: the sponsor was a Democrat joined by a Florida Republican, with 9 total cosponsors including 2 Republicans; no record shows organized opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have closed new leasing in the Atlantic planning areas, the Straits of Florida, and part of the eastern Gulf until mid-2029, removing acreage the industry could otherwise bid on. Drilling activity and spill risk in those waters run directly against the interests of the tourism and fishing economies that share the same coastline.
Beach towns and coastal businesses depend on clean water and unspoiled shorelines; keeping new drilling rigs and the risk of a spill away protects the beaches, views, and water quality they sell.
Seismic surveying, rigs, and especially an oil spill threaten fish stocks and fishing grounds along the Atlantic and eastern Gulf; the moratorium shields those fisheries.
